transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-06-23 11:00 PDT / 18:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan Park, Maya Brooks (Redwood); Dr. Lena Ortiz, Jamal Reed, Sofia Kim, Ben Cho (Polaris)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Polaris is evaluating reserved GPU capacity for inference serving of a genomics model suite. Primary concerns: isolation/tenantization, burst handling (prewarm + hot pool), latency SLOs for interactive research vs batch scoring, and security/compliance (KMS, audit logs, SOC2 evidence). Team leaned toward dedicated but needs cost comparisons vs hosted and a clear failover plan. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing worksheet, burst playbook, and Polaris to share traffic profile and compliance answers.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and latency targets
- Workload characteristics (seq length, batch vs interactive)
- Isolation: single-tenant vs multi-tenant on Dedicated
- Burst strategy: hot-pools, prewarming, fallback to hosted
- Security: KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs, data residency
- Timeline and procurement constraints

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood, AE on the West coast. Maya from our solutions engineering team's with me. How's your afternoon, Lena?
[00:08] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Good, hey Ethan, hi Maya. Thanks — excited to dig in. We have Jamal and Sofia and Ben on the call to cover infra and security.
[00:14] Jamal Reed: Yep, hi all. Quick context: we're moving from a proof-of-concept on a cluster of A10s to something that can handle production, so reserved's on the table.
[00:22] Maya Brooks: Great, can you — quick ask — can you share the most important SLA you need? p95 latency, throughput, anything like that?
[00:28] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Two buckets — interactive research UI (~200–400ms p95) for clinicians and scientists; and batch variant scoring with higher throughput, can accept higher latency, like 2–5s. We also have occasional spikes when a pipeline replays thousands of sequences.
[00:44] Ben Cho: And to add, we run some on-prem models in air-gapped environments for PHI — so we need private options too, but first priority is getting production quality for cloud workloads.
[00:55] Ethan Park: Understood. For the interactive SLO you'll probably want GPU types with good latency at small batch sizes and a prewarm strategy. For bursts we have hot-pools and a couple of fallback routes — either burst to hosted capacity or auto-scale dedicated if you have reserved headroom.
[01:12] Jamal Reed: How deterministic is that? We need predictable latency during a spike. We can't have the UX degrade during demos to clinicians.
[01:19] Maya Brooks: Right, so in Dedicated we recommend reserved pools sized for steady-state and then configure a small hot-pool for rapid prewarmed instances. The fallback to hosted is best-effort for traffic above reserved+hot-pool. You can also pin critical routes to single-tenant nodes for strict isolation so noisy tenants can't evict your capacity.
[01:38] Sofia Kim: When you say "single-tenant nodes" what's actually isolated? Is it compute only or do you get isolated networking and storage? We need VPC-level isolation and KMS integration.
[01:48] Maya Brooks: Good point. Dedicated offers node-level tenancy for compute isolation, and when you combine it with Redwood Private (VPC package) you get customer-managed networking, private endpoints, and KMS/HSM integration. With that deployment model, logs and audit trails can also be forwarded to your SIEM.
[02:05] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Okay, timeline — procurement wants numbers by end of quarter, and security would like SOC2 evidence and the KMS docs. How long to get that?
[02:14] Ethan Park: We can share SOC2 certs and our security pack today — I'll attach the link after the call. Pricing and reserved worksheet I'll get to you by Thursday. For Private deployments the timeline is longer — usually 6–10 weeks depending on networking and cert handoffs.
[02:28] Jamal Reed: Got it. Can you talk about cost math for reserved vs hosted? We tried hosted during POC and it was fine, but cost at scale looked high.
[02:36] Maya Brooks: Absolutely. The simplified way to think about it: hosted = pay-as-you-go, best for variable/low steady usage; reserved = commit to capacity, big unit cost savings for steady baseline. Then you layer burst policies — the reserved pool for baseline and a hot pool + hosted for overflow. We have a workbook that models QPS, token length, and cost per token for several GPU families.
[02:55] Ben Cho: Is the hot-pool always reserved? Or is it more like prewarmed ephemeral nodes?
[03:00] Maya Brooks: Hot-pool is ephemeral but prewarmed — you can size it and keep it warm for minutes to hours depending on your appetite for cost. It's cheaper than keeping all of your reserved pool conservatively large, but it does cost more than strict idle reserved nodes.
[03:15] Dr. Lena Ortiz: I also want to understand model variants and fallbacks: if we quantize models for cheaper inference and accuracy drops, can the system fall back to a higher-fidelity model?
[03:25] Maya Brooks: Yes — Redwood supports policy-based routing by model version and fidelity. You can set A/B rollouts and automatic fallback to a more accurate variant if quality checks fail or if latency thresholds are violated. We tie that into evals so you can detect regressions.
[03:40] Jamal Reed: Network egress — we need to ensure we don't accidentally route PHI through hosted endpoints. How do we prevent that?
[03:46] Ethan Park: For PHI workflows you should use Private deployments or on-prem package. On the hosted side we have strict data handling, but we cannot guarantee non-ejection to public endpoints for PHI. So for regulated data you should choose Dedicated+Private.
[03:58] Sofia Kim: Ok that's consistent with our security stance. Also logging — can audit logs be exported to our Splunk or Azure Sentinel?
[04:05] Maya Brooks: Yes, audit logs can be exported via syslog/HTTPS to your SIEM, and we support log redaction rules and field-level encryption for sensitive fields. We'll include config examples in the security pack.
[04:18] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Can you walk us through an example scenario — say 2x baseline traffic for 15 minutes, what happens?
[04:24] Maya Brooks: Sure. Baseline served from reserved pool. Spike hits — hot-pool immediate capacity absorbs first delta. If still over provisioned, route policy kicks in: non-critical batch routes get deprioritized, interactive routes get routed to reserved+hot-pool first; if still over, we have two options you can choose: 1) automatically spill-over to Redwood hosted endpoints (best-effort, may see higher latency), or 2) shed non-critical requests or throttle to preserve SLOs.
[04:48] Ben Cho: Any chance we can do a prewarm choreography with Kubernetes jobs to spin nodes up faster on our side?
[04:54] Maya Brooks: You can run local prewarm scripts but it's often better to use Redwood's prewarm API — it's optimized for cache warming and KV priming. It takes care of the heavy KV cache population to avoid the cold-start penalty.
[05:06] Jamal Reed: KV cache — do you persist KV cache across restarts if the node is reclaimed? We can't afford to rebuild embedding caches every time.
[05:13] Maya Brooks: For Dedicated you'd typically keep a warm cache in the hot-pool; for longer-lived persistence we support warm snapshot restore to accelerate cold starts. There are tradeoffs, and we can show numbers from similar customers in the workbook.
[05:27] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Great. On compliance, Sofia, anything we need to call out?
[05:30] Sofia Kim: We need KMS integration for key separation, SSO via SAML, RBAC, and the ability to run a periodic access review. Also retention policies for logs — at least 7 years for certain audit trails.
[05:41] Ethan Park: We support external KMS, SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and long-term log retention as an add-on. I'll point you to the compliance pack.
[05:50] Jamal Reed: How about cold-start latency numbers — can you share numbers for Llama2-ish LLMs at 8k tokens and typical throughput?
[05:58] Maya Brooks: We have benchmark profiles in our model catalog with measured p95s for common families. For 8k seqs, latency is dominated by token processing and memory bandwidth; typical cold-start for large models can be 5–15s but with prewarm and KV priming we reduce perceived cold start to subsecond for interactive routes. We'll attach the catalog snapshot.
[06:20] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[06:23] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Can you run a short pilot where you host a warm pool sized to our baseline and we generate a synthetic spike? We want to measure tail latency under our real prompt distribution.
[06:32] Ethan Park: Yes, we can do a pilot (PCT - pilot capacity test) — usually 2–4 weeks. We can provision a dedicated pool for the pilot and run a synthetic spike with your traffic. Cost for pilot is usually credited if you convert to reserved.
[06:44] Jamal Reed: And procurement — we need clear SLA terms and an escalation path.
[06:49] Ethan Park: Our dedicated contracts include SLA targets and a named escalation contact. We'll include the standard SLR/SLA in the pricing packet.
[06:58] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Let's make sure we have an on-call handover if we do a pilot, and a runbook for who to call.
[07:05] Maya Brooks: We'll provide a runbook and an on-call rotation for Redwood-side ops during the pilot window.
[07:12] Ben Cho: One more nit — what about GPU families? We tested on A100 but we might move to H100s for perf. Do you manage model re-compiles for different kernels?
[07:21] Maya Brooks: Yes, our runtime has a compilation layer and selects optimized kernels based on the GPU family. We will profile on H100 and provide perf estimates and cost deltas. Recompile is handled by our infra side; sometimes we need a short model onboarding step.
[07:35] Jamal Reed: Any reseller partners in EMEA for procurement? We sometimes need local PO/CD terms.
[07:41] Ethan Park: We do have partners in EMEA, and I'm happy to loop in partners/sales ops in the follow-up.
[07:48] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Cool. Anything on observability — token-level cost breakdown, traces?
[07:53] Maya Brooks: Yes, Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency per route, traces, and model-level dashboards. You can export traces to OpenTelemetry collectors.
[08:03] Ethan Park: Ok, quick recap before we run through the last 40 minutes with details and Qs: action items — I'll send pricing and SOC2 pack, Maya will send burst playbook and prewarm runbook, Lena will share traffic profile. We also agreed a pilot might be valuable.
[08:20] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Yep, thanks.

[08:30] -- technical deep dive starts --
[08:32] Maya Brooks: I'll walk through the hot-pool vs reserved sizing example. Slide references: 1) reserved sizing formula, 2) hot-pool cost curve, 3) fallback routing. Link: https://redwood.app/links/reserved-capacity-deck
[08:47] Maya Brooks: If your baseline is 120 concurrent interactive sessions and median tokens per req is 350, our recommended reserved capacity for A100s is X nodes (we'll compute exact number in the worksheet). Key knobs are: prewarm interval, hot-pool size, and max-hosted-fallback percentage.
[09:12] Jamal Reed: For prewarm interval, do you typically keep it alive minutes or hours? Our usage is spiky throughout the day with 20–30 minute spikes.
[09:20] Maya Brooks: For that pattern we recommend keeping hot-pool alive for at least an hour during business hours and enable short-term prewarm for off-hours bursts. It's a cost vs latency trade. We'll show cost simulations.
[09:34] Ben Cho: Any guidance on quantization vs accuracy? Our genomics models are sensitive to small changes.
[09:40] Maya Brooks: For sensitive models we recommend mixed strategy: CPU or int8 for non-critical batch, while interactive calls use fp16 or bfloat16 with higher fidelity. We can also route a small sample of traffic to the quantized model for A/B testing and monitor eval metrics.
[09:55] Dr. Lena Ortiz: About rollbacks — if the quantized model regresses on key prompts, can we do immediate rollback?
[10:00] Maya Brooks: Yes, model rollouts are atomic and we have automatic rollback policies based on eval thresholds. That can be integrated with your monitoring too.
[10:10] Jamal Reed: Anything else on networking — do we need to open egress ports for prewarm callbacks?
[10:15] Maya Brooks: For Private deployments you'll open a few endpoints for the control plane; we'll provide a minimal firewall rule set. For Hosted/Dedicated hybrid you can use VPC peering or private link.
[10:27] Sofia Kim: For the audit log retention you mentioned 7 years — is that an add-on? What's pricing?
[10:33] Ethan Park: Long-term log retention is an add-on; pricing depends on retention size and ingest rate. I'll put an example in the pricing worksheet.
[10:40] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Alright, timeline check — procurement wants numbers by EOM. We need a pilot runbook this week if possible.
[10:47] Ethan Park: We'll prioritize the pilot runbook; Maya will draft it today and I'll send pricing.
[10:53] Jamal Reed: Can you include a recommended hot-pool config for our baseline in the worksheet?
[10:58] Maya Brooks: Yes, we'll include a recommended config plus an array of trade-off options.
[11:05] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Ok, I think that's the major list. Anything else?
[11:09] Ben Cho: One more: incident response — can you share a sample postmortem template for incidents involving model regressions?
[11:15] Maya Brooks: Sure — we'll attach our incident template and sample playbook.
[11:20] Ethan Park: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts discussed.
[11:25] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
